newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippines shields currency from Thai woes.
newsitem.headline: Philippines shields currency from Thai woes.

text.p: The Philippines, fearing its markets would suffer after Thailand floated the baht, on Wednesday sold hundreds of millions of dollars and forced up interest rates to shield its own currency.
"We have to do something (to defend the peso)," Central Bank Governor Gabriel Singson told Reuters after Thailand's move on Wednesday morning.

Thailand announced its exchange rate system would be a managed float from July 2, a step analysts said was an effective devaluation of the baht. The Thai central bank also lifted its key commercial bank lending rate by two percentage points to 12.5 percent in a bid to support its currency.
Since April, the Philippines has repeatedly defended its currency and stock market from speculative attacks as investors bet that the country's economy could mirror Thailand's financial crisis.

Thailand's announcement had sparked a sharp weakening of the Philippine currency against the dollar. The peso steadied only with the help of heavy dollar selling by the Central Bank and sharply higher interest rates.

The one-day reverse repurchase agreement rate was boosted twice during the morning with the second increase taking the rate to 24 percent, up from 15 percent when the paper was last offered three weeks ago.
The rate serves as an indicator of the closely watched Central Bank overnight interest rate.
Turnover in the Manila peso market surged to more than 800 million dollars in the morning, its highest on record.
Traders estimated that more than half that amount was in Central Bank dollar sales.
By midday, the peso was quoted at 26.379 to the dollar, little changed from the previous close. The currency had weakened to 26.380 in early trade.
Concerns over the peso also battered the foreign-dominated Philippine stock market. The composite index tumbled almost two percent to end at 2,764.89.
"You should expect some initial spillover effect. I am very confident this will settle down," the Central Bank's Singson said.
But he warned that the Bank would take any measures it thought necessary to beat off speculators and to keep the peso stable.
"We are determined to defend our currency," Singson said.

"We have shown our determination in the past to defend the currency from speculative attacks. This is a speculative attack on the currency resulting from what happened in Thailand...it is not affecting the fundamentals. The fundamentals are still good."

But bankers warned that persistently high interest rates to defend the peso -- whose stability the Central Bank considers crucial to keep inflation under control -- could hurt the economy in the longer-term.
"It might be too expensive in the long-term. Something's got to give," Banco Santander Treasurer Antonio Agcaoili said.

There have already been signs that the country's manufacturing industry is not doing as well as expected and many economists doubt the economy will reach the government's target of seven percent growth this year.
Exporters have also been asking the government to allow a weaker peso to lift the competitiveness of their products in overseas markets.
